s: Which one of the following processes is not a part of long-wave radiation?
x: Conduction, convection and radiation are the heat-transfer processes tied to long-wave (terrestrial) radiation, whereas scattering is a shortwave process, so Scattering is the odd one out.

s: Troposphere is the hottest part of the atmosphere because
o: it is closet to the Sun.
it is heated by the Earth’s surface.
there are charged particles in it.
x: The troposphere is heated from below by long-wave radiation re-emitted by the earth's surface, not directly by the sun or by heat generated within it.

s: Wind is often found to blow in a hot summer day due to
o: conduction of heat between air and soil on the Earth.
x: Wind on a hot day arises from convection: warm air rises, and cooler air flows in to replace it. Conduction only heats the thin layer of air touching the ground.

s: Which of the following does not require a medium?
x: Radiation transfers heat by electromagnetic waves and needs no medium, whereas conduction and convection need matter (solid or fluid) to carry heat.

s: Which one of the following correctly describes insolation?
o: Vertical transfer of heat by rising air
Horizontal transfer of heat by moving air
Direct heating of the atmosphere by outgoing long-wave radiation
Direct heating by incoming short-wave solar radiation
x: Insolation is the direct heating received from incoming short-wave solar radiation.

s: What is the horizontal transfer of heat by wind called?
x: Advection is the horizontal transfer of heat by wind; vertical transfer by rising warm air is convection.

s: The Loo, a hot wind of northern India, is an example of which of the following processes?
x: The Loo transfers heat horizontally through moving air and is therefore an example of advection.

s: By which of the following is the atmosphere mainly heated?
o: Direct absorption of incoming short-wave solar radiation
Outgoing long-wave terrestrial radiation from below
x: The atmosphere is largely transparent to incoming short-wave radiation but absorbs outgoing long-wave terrestrial radiation, so it is heated mainly from below.

s: Why does temperature normally decrease with increasing altitude?
o: Higher air receives more long-wave radiation from the Sun.
The ground heats the air from below, while higher air is thinner and contains less water vapour and dust.
The Earth stops emitting radiation above the lower atmosphere.
The atmosphere is heated mainly from above by direct solar radiation.
x: The ground heats the atmosphere from below. At higher levels the air is thinner and contains less water vapour and dust, so it absorbs less heat.

s: Which sky condition produces the greatest terrestrial cooling at night?
x: Clear skies allow more daytime solar heating and more night-time terrestrial cooling, whereas clouds cut both.

s: In what form is terrestrial radiation, the main heater of the atmosphere, emitted?
x: The Earth re-emits heat as long-wave infra-red radiation, which heats the air from below.

s: Which gases mainly absorb the long-wave radiation re-emitted by the Earth?
x: Carbon dioxide and water vapour absorb the Earth's long-wave infra-red radiation.

s: Which of the following pairs of heating process and mechanism is correctly matched?
o: Conduction – Heats the lower layers of air
Insolation – Long-wave heat from the Earth
x: Conduction heats the lower air in contact with warm ground; advection is horizontal, convection vertical and insolation short-wave.

s: Which parts of the Earth’s surface experience least variation in incoming solar radiation throughout the year?
x: Equatorial regions get direct rays and nearly constant day length all year, so their insolation varies least. Polar and high-latitude areas have large seasonal swings.

s: The intensity of insolation depends on
x: Insolation depends mainly on the angle of the sun's rays, which is set by latitude: it is highest where rays are direct and falls toward the poles.

s: The greatest seasonal contrast of insolation on the Earth is in which of the following latitudinal zones?
x: Polar zones have the greatest seasonal contrast in insolation, with months of continuous daylight in summer and none in winter, whereas the equator is nearly constant.

s: Radiations coming from the sun are mostly in the form of
o: Both short and long wavelength infrared.
x: Solar radiation is mostly visible light plus short-wavelength (near) infrared. Long-wave infrared is what the earth re-emits, not what comes from the sun.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about insolation?
o: The angle of the Sun's rays affects the insolation received at a place.
The length of the day affects the insolation received at a place.
Atmospheric transparency has no effect on the insolation received.
The slope and aspect of the land affect the insolation received.
x: Atmospheric transparency does influence insolation, along with the angle of the rays, duration of sunshine, and slope and aspect of land.

s: Which one of the following correctly represents the Earth's aphelion?
x: Aphelion occurs around 4 July, when the Earth is approximately 152 million kilometres from the Sun.

s: Why do the highest temperatures on Earth generally occur in the sub-tropical deserts rather than at the Equator?
o: The maximum annual rainfall of the deserts
The permanent presence of cold ocean currents
Persistent cloud cover and humid air
x: Sub-tropical deserts around 20°–30° N have clear skies and dry air, permitting very high temperatures; the Equator does not record the highest temperatures merely because it receives strong insolation.

s: At the same latitude, insolation is generally higher over:
o: Polar seas than over tropical land
x: Insolation declines towards the poles and, at the same latitude, is higher over continents than over oceans.

s: In the Earth's heat budget, where is a heat surplus found?
x: The tropics have a heat surplus and the poles a deficit; winds and ocean currents carry heat poleward.

s: What type of the Sun's rays does the equator receive, causing it to be heated more than the poles?
x: Latitude sets the Sun's angle: the equator gets more direct rays and greater heating, while the poles get oblique rays and lower heating.

s: On about which date is the Earth at perihelion, its closest point to the Sun?
x: Perihelion falls around 3 January (about 147 million km); aphelion around 4 July.

s: What is the approximate Earth–Sun distance at perihelion?
x: The Earth is about 147 million km from the Sun at perihelion and about 152 million km at aphelion.

s: How does insolation received at the Earth's surface generally change from the Equator towards the poles?
x: The Equator gets direct rays and the poles oblique rays, so insolation falls poleward.

s: Which one of the following is associated with 'Albedo'?

Land covered with fresh snow has a high albedo (75-95%), most sunlight hitting the surface bounces back towards space. The average albedo of Earth is the 30%. The sand desert has an albedo of 20-30%. s: After fresh snow, which of the following surfaces has the highest albedo?

s: Which clouds tend to reflect incoming sunlight and produce cooling?

s: What does the albedo of a surface refer to?

amount of heat stored below the surface
rate at which terrestrial radiation is emitted
amount of moisture absorbed by the surface

increases the albedo of the exposed ocean
exposes a darker ocean surface that absorbs more heat
prevents the ocean from absorbing solar radiation
x: Melting ice exposes dark ocean water, which has a lower albedo and absorbs more heat, producing a positive ice-albedo feedback.

s: What effect do high, thin clouds generally have?
o: Raise the Earth's albedo the most
x: High, thin clouds trap heat (warming), while low, thick clouds reflect sunlight (cooling).

s: What is the approximate albedo of fresh snow?
x: Fresh snow reflects 75–95% of incoming radiation; dry sand 20–40%, crop land 15–25% and water below 10%.

x: Of the 35 reflected units, clouds reflect 27, scattering 6 and snow and ice 2.

x: Of 100 units, 35 are reflected to space, 14 absorbed by the atmosphere and 51 by the Earth's surface.

s: Of the 51 units absorbed by the Earth's surface, how many are radiated directly to space?
x: The surface radiates 17 units directly to space and 34 to the atmosphere.

s: Of 100 units of insolation, how many are absorbed by the atmosphere?
x: Of 100 units, 35 are reflected, 14 absorbed by the atmosphere and 51 by the surface.

s: What do the 35 units of insolation reflected back to space form?
x: The 35 units reflected by clouds, scattering and snow and ice make up the planetary albedo.

s: In the Earth's heat budget, how many units does the atmosphere radiate to space?
x: The atmosphere sends 48 units (14 + 34) to space; with 17 from the surface, 65 units go out.

s: The January isotherm taken as a basis for dividing India into tropical and sub-tropical zones is
x: The standard January isotherm used to distinguish India's tropical (southern) and subtropical (northern) regions is the 18°C line. s:
Consider the following statements
1.
Statement I: In January, in the Northern Hemisphere, the isotherms bend equatorward while crossing the landmasses, and poleward while crossing the oceans.

During winter, landmasses cool more rapidly than oceans due to differences in heat capacity. Isotherms reflect these temperature Physical Geography PMF IAS Geo – 12 gradients, bending to reflect colder temperatures over land and warmer temperatures over oceans. Specifically, isotherms shift equatorward (southward) over landmasses, indicating colder temperatures, and poleward (northward) over oceans, indicating warmer temperatures, due to the moderating effect of oceans. boundary between the tropical and polar zones, fixed at 23½° latitude.
line joining the coldest places in both hemispheres.
geographical Equator, which never shifts seasonally.

reflect back heat given off by Earth

x: Without an atmosphere there would be no greenhouse blanket to retain heat at night, so Earth's surface would lose heat rapidly (about -18°C average instead of +15°C), and daytime heating would go unmoderated. Day-night extremes would therefore increase.

Which of the following latitudes (north or south) would you associate with 'Horse Latitudes' ?
x: The horse latitudes are located at about 30° to 35° north and south of the Equator. In the northern hemisphere it is called the north subtropical high-pressure belt and in the southern hemisphere, it is known as the south subtropical high-pressure belt. The existence of these pressure belts is due to the fact that the rising air of the equatorial region is deflected towards poles due to the earth’s rotation. After becoming cold and heavy, it descends in these regions due to Earth rotation and gets piled up. This results in high pressure. Calm conditions with feeble and variable winds are found here. In ancient times vessels with a cargo of horses passing through these belts found difficulty in sailing under these calm conditions. They used to throw a few horses in to the sea in order to make the vessels lighter. Thus, these belts or latitudes came to be known as ‘horse latitudes’.

2. Tibetan highland divides jet stream into North and South Branches.

x: During the winter, a distinct pattern of air circulation is observed higher up in the atmosphere. Significantly, westerly winds continue to affect western and central Asia extending approx. 9 to 13 km from west to east. At latitudes north of the Himalayas and almost parallel to the Tibetan highlands, these winds blow across the Asian continent. Thus the first statement is true. Notably, these jet streams are obstructed by the hills of Tibet consequently, jet stream splits in two. One of its branches flows north of the Tibetan highlands and the other, which originates south of the Himalayas, blows eastward before merging again to form a single stream over China, Hence statement 2 is correct. Notably, the northern branch of jet stream does not play an important role in winter weather in India. So statement (3) is false.
